source.title: Compositional Concept-Based Neuron-Level Interpretability for Deep Reinforcement Learning
source.authors: Ze-Yu Jiang; Hai Huang; Xingquan Zuo

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The arXiv version date in the text is later than the stated publication year, but this does not affect extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies neuron-level concept alignment in DRL, but does not test or rely on superposition, polysemanticity, SAE features, or feature dimensionality as defined by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: Figure 2 reports a width/depth analysis of mean neuron-concept Jaccard similarity. This is related to interpretability and network capacity, but does not measure feature sharing, polysemanticity, or superposition; record it under fits_no_version. The paper also reports explanation and perturbation results, but these do not bear on the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study builds a neuron-level compositional concept explanation method for small DQN agents (Blackjack, LunarLander). It never mentions superposition, polysemanticity as capacity sharing, SAEs, or feature dimensionality. None of its results measure features stored in overlapping directions, or polysemanticity attributed to a cause. 'Discusses' is the loosest available relation: the paper neither tests nor cites the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that the framework yields interpretable neuron-level logical explanations in Blackjack-v1 and LunarLander-v3. They claim targeted perturbations confirm a causal role for the identified concepts.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a DRL neuron-explanation method and does not reproduce or apply the original superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Mean neuron-concept Jaccard similarity decreases monotonically with network width; depth 3 achieves optimal alignment in the depth comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: In DQN agents, mean neuron-concept Jaccard similarity falls monotonically as width grows from 64 to 512. Depth 3 gives the highest alignment, and all configurations solve the task. The authors attribute this to task knowledge becoming 'distributed across more units'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small DRL value networks, best-match neuron-concept alignment decreases with width at equal task performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Some penultimate-layer neurons are best explained by disjunctive formulas over unrelated state variables. Neuron 41 has J=0.999 for a formula combining altitude, lateral velocity, angular velocity and leg contact; the authors call it 'multimodal'. No capacity analysis is given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small DRL networks contain neurons whose activation is best described by disjunctions of distinct state concepts, i.e. mixed selectivity.

record.code_released: not stated (the text says the implementation is publicly available through a GitHub Repository, but gives no URL)
record.problems: The architecture-analysis values are presented in a figure without exact numbers or uncertainty estimates. The paper's experiments cover two DRL environments and do not directly measure the claim's feature-sharing or superposition constructs.
record.rows_left_out: None. The rows record the width and depth conditions in Figure 2; the paper's neuron examples and perturbation outcomes do not measure any listed claim version.

untested.parts: All: no toy sparse-feature setup, no feature-direction geometry, no sparsity transition.
All: polysemanticity is not linked to capacity or feature importance. The width sweep measures concept alignment, not feature sharing.
All: disjunctive ('multimodal') neurons are reported, but their cause is not analysed.
All: no LLMs, no measurement of distributed features, no dictionary learning.
All: features are not analysed as directions of any dimensionality.

record.verdict_notes: There are no verdicts because no version is tested. The width-sweep result might look superficially relevant to V2: wider networks show less neuron-concept alignment, the opposite of what a capacity-pressure intuition about monosemanticity would predict. However, Jaccard best-match alignment is not a polysemanticity or superposition measure, and no features-versus-dimensions analysis is done, so it is recorded under fits_no_version. Neuron 41's disjunctive formula is likewise noted there rather than as V3 evidence, because the study does not address why the neuron is mixed.

versions.untested_parts: No test of sparse features exceeding dimensions, overlapping directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
No test of polysemanticity arising from limited feature capacity, feature competition, or importance-dependent dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of polysemanticity arising from mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
No LLM activation analysis, feature spreading measurement, or sparse-feature dictionary recovery.
No test of whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical model units.
No test of whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.
